title: How much is it?
goal: Go shopping: ask prices, haggle, name colors and sizes — and mark a specific object with the ending *-i*.
bekal: ask the price with *ne kadar* and *kaça*

dialogs.title: Dialogue — Kapalıçarşı'da
dialogs.intro: Inside the Grand Bazaar. Budi stops in front of a scarf stall. The seller, Hakan, has had his eye on him for a while.

lines.speaker: Hakan:
lines.text: Buyurun abi, hoş geldiniz! Bakın, çok güzel şallar.
lines.id: Come in, brother, welcome! Look, beautiful scarves.

lines.id: Can I see that blue one?

lines.speaker: Hakan:

notes: **Haggling is expected in the covered bazaars, not in ordinary shops.** In the Kapalıçarşı, the Mısır Çarşısı (Spice Bazaar) and tourist stalls, the first price really is inflated. In supermarkets, pharmacies, restaurants and shops with price tags, haggling is considered odd.

**Olur mu? is the key to haggling.** Literally "does it work?" — used to propose a number. The answer is *olur* (OK) or *olmaz* (no way). These two words settle almost every small negotiation in Turkey.

**Sellers call male customers abi and female customers abla** — even when the customer is older. It's the friendly language of trade, not family. Don't be offended, and don't feel you have to return it.
**Maviyi, not mavi.** Because he means a specific scarf that's being pointed at, the word gets the object ending *-yi*. That's this unit's grammar point, and the one foreign learners skip most often.

sections.title: The ending -i: marking a specific object

blocks.text: Turkish has no word for "the", but it does have a way to tell **a specific thing** from **any thing** — the ending *-i / -ı / -u / -ü* on the object of the sentence.

head: Without the ending
With the ending
The difference
rows: I'm reading a book / I'm reading THE book
I'm drinking tea / I'm drinking THE tea
We're watching a movie / THE movie

blocks.text: The practical rule: use the ending when **the listener knows which thing you mean** — because it's been mentioned, pointed at, or there's only one. Without the ending, the sentence talks about a kind of thing, not an item.

items: **Names of people and places**: *Ayşe'yi görüyorum* (I see Ayşe), *İstanbul'u seviyorum*.
**Things that already have a possessive ending**: *çantamı*, *evini*, *arabasını*.

blocks.title: The most common mistake
items: Beginners often put *-i* on EVERY object. So *Su içiyorum* (I'm drinking water) becomes *Suyu içiyorum* — which means "I'm drinking THE water", and sounds as if you're pointing at a particular glass in front of someone.
When in doubt, leave the ending off. Turkish forgives an under-marked object more readily than an over-marked one.

head: Türkçe
Say it
English
rows: Any chance of a small discount?

blocks.text: *Düşünüyorum* — "I'm thinking" — is the most polite way to leave without buying. It's understood as a gentle no, and a good seller won't chase you after that.
*Kahverengi* literally means "coffee color" — *kahve* + *rengi*. The same pattern is used for other colors named after things: *gül rengi* (rose color), *deniz mavisi* (sea blue).

blocks.title: Adjectives always come before the noun
items: *Mavi şal* (a blue scarf), *büyük ev* (a big house), *güzel bir gün* (a beautiful day). Note that *bir* goes BETWEEN the adjective and the noun, not in front of both: *güzel bir gün*, not *bir güzel gün*.
When the adjective is the predicate, it moves to the end and takes a person ending: *Bu şal mavi.* (This scarf is blue.) *Yorgunum.* (I'm tired.)

items: Cover the Turkish and rebuild it from memory: "What time is it now?" · "Classes start on Monday." · "I study every day." · "When's the exam?" · "I don't work on the weekend."
